explainBack.prompt: Why might Muse send an email on your behalf without asking you at that moment, even though Meta advertises approval prompts?
explainBack.response: Approvals are governed by a control outside the agent that matches each proposed action against the permission you already granted for that service. Permissions can be one-time, task- or session-limited, time-bounded or permanent, and previously allowed, read-only or low-risk actions may proceed without any fresh prompt. So if you earlier granted a lasting send permission, the control finds the action within scope and lets it through — the prompt only appears when the action falls outside what you already allowed.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: P005 (external control checks proposed action against the service's permission) and P006 (grant types, control chooses which to offer, previously allowed/low-risk actions proceed without interruption; prompts are design, not guarantee).
explainBack.assessment: Accurate: the article's mechanism fully supports this causal answer in ordinary language, including the reason prompts are not universal.

unseenTransfer.prompt: Using the article's mechanism, what access should she grant and what should she expect the system to do at each step?
unseenTransfer.response: Per the article, each connected service is a separate decision, and read and action access can differ. Watching statements needs only read access, so she should grant read-only — the article says read-only actions may then proceed without repeated prompts. Cancelling and messaging the bank are actions that change her account, so she should grant those, if at all, as a one-time or task-limited permission rather than a permanent one; the outside control will check each proposed cancellation against that scope before it reaches the internet. Because the agent will make mistakes and prompt injection is open, she should verify the cancellation in the audit trail, and remember today's workspace does not block Meta's own access — sensitive financial data sits under the current, weaker privacy regime until the promised user-key version ships.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: P006 (scoped grants, read-only uninterrupted), P005 (external check per service), P007 (mistakes, prompt injection), P009 (read/action decision, audit trail), P008/P010 (current Meta access versus later promise).
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism resolves this novel banking scenario completely, including the risk posture — strong evidence the explanation transfers beyond its own examples.

incidentExplained.observation: What launched, where, how it acts, what governs it and what is still promised form a complete causal sequence across P002-P008.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: Meta launched Muse, a personal AI agent, in the United States on September 8. It is rolling out through iOS, Android and muse.ai; Meta also says people can message it in WhatsApp. Most use is free, with subscriptions for more, but the reviewed launch material gives no exact limit or price.
Muse works in a separate cloud workspace. Meta says a control outside the agent checks whether a proposed action fits the permission for that connected service before letting it reach the internet.

The current workspace separates one person’s agent and data from other users. Meta says it may still access data to operate, support or secure the service, and that interactions may train later models unless the person opts out. For later this year, Meta promises a version encrypted with a key only the user holds, intended to keep the workspace inaccessible even to Meta. It remains with trusted testers.

termsExplainedInContext.observation: 'Personal AI agent' is defined at first use (P004) and 'prompt injection' is defined inline at first mention (P007).

artifactEvidence.excerpt: A personal AI agent is software that can plan and take several actions toward a personal goal rather than only answer once. Meta’s example combines turning an Instagram recipe into a grocery list with sending a dinner invitation. Email is a separate permission choice: Meta says people can allow Muse to read email without allowing it to send.

Meta’s safety post says the agent will make mistakes and that prompt injection—malicious instructions hidden in material an agent reads—remains an open problem. AP confirmed the launch and explained the agent-versus-chatbot distinction, but did not test Muse’s safeguards or reliability.

readerConsequenceSpecific.observation: The consequence lands on a specific reader situation: what access to grant email or a purchase service, and which privacy limit applies today.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: A fresh approval does not appear before everything. Meta says a person can let Muse read email without letting it send. Permissions may be one-time, limited to a task or session, time-bounded or permanent; the control system chooses which options to offer. Previously allowed, read-only or low-risk actions may proceed without interruption. Email and purchase prompts are Meta’s design, not a guarantee that Muse always behaves correctly.

Before connecting a service, decide what this task needs: read access, action access or no access. If Muse offers a one-time or task-limited permission, use it when a lasting grant is unnecessary. Meta says its audit trail and connection settings let you inspect actions and change or remove access.

The next useful evidence is independent testing of real actions and safeguards, plus general availability of the promised private workspace. Until then, distinguish today’s limits on Meta access from the later promise to prevent that access.
